x: Article 85, in Part V, governs summoning, prorogation and dissolution. Article 123 deals with ordinances, and Part VI with State Legislatures.
t: Recall Article 85 for sessions and Article 123 for ordinances.

x: Under Article 85, the President summons each House at such time and place as they think fit, acting on ministerial advice. Presiding officers only adjourn sittings.
t: Discriminate the President's summoning power from the presiding officers' adjournment.

x: Article 85 says six months must not pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next. So Parliament meets at least twice a year.
t: Recall the six-month rule of Article 85.

x: Option D is incorrect: the Constitution sets no fixed number of sessions. It only sets a gap of at most six months (so at least two sessions a year); the Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions are a convention.
t: Discriminate the constitutional six-month rule from the three-session convention.

x: Both are false: the Constitution prescribes no minimum number of sitting days, and the Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions are a convention, not a mandate.
t: Remember that Article 85 sets only the six-month limit.

x: Adjournment pauses a sitting for a set time, adjournment sine die ends it without naming a day, prorogation ends the session, and dissolution ends the Lok Sabha itself. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Rank the four by how much they end: sitting, session, House.

x: The presiding officer adjourns a sitting for a set time and adjourns sine die without naming a day. The President prorogues under Article 85(2)(a) and dissolves the Lok Sabha under Article 85(2)(b). The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Separate presiding-officer actions from presidential ones, then use the clause numbers.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Adjournment
(b) Adjournment sine die
(c) Prorogation
(d) Dissolution

List-II
(i) President of India under Article 85(2)(b)
(ii) Presiding Officer, suspending a sitting for a specified time
(iii) President of India under Article 85(2)(a)
(iv) Presiding Officer, ending a sitting without naming a day of reassembly

x: Adjournment pauses a sitting for hours, days or weeks. The session continues and pending business stays alive. Prorogation ends the session itself.
t: Discriminate pausing a sitting from ending a session.

x: I, III and IV are correct: Article 85 covers summoning, 85(2)(a) prorogation and 85(2)(b) dissolution. II is false because the six-month gap is in Article 85; Article 123 is about ordinances.
t: Check which Article each limit belongs to.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 85 deals with the summoning and sessions of Parliament.
II. Article 123 specifies the maximum interval between two parliamentary sessions.
III. Article 85(2)(a) relates to prorogation.
IV. Article 85(2)(b) relates to dissolution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: an ordinance can be issued just after a session ends, Parliament may not meet for up to six months, and the ordinance lapses six weeks after it reassembles. R explains A.
t: Add the six-month session gap to the six-week reassembly limit.

x: Three are real limits: the six-month session gap, six weeks after reassembly for an ordinance, and an ordinance's six-month-six-week life. No minimum of 100 sitting days is prescribed.
t: Find the invented sitting-day minimum.

x: Option C is incorrect: periods of prorogation are left out when counting the 60 days of absence under Article 101(4), and so are adjournments of more than four consecutive days.
t: Recall what is excluded from the 60-day absence count.

x: Three are correct: adjournment does not affect the session, adjournment sine die comes before prorogation, and the President prorogues on ministerial advice. III is false because prorogation does not end pending bills; only notices lapse.
t: Discriminate what lapses on prorogation from what lapses on dissolution.

x: I, III and IV are correct: dissolution ends the Lok Sabha and its pending business lapses (subject to Article 107), but the Rajya Sabha is permanent. II is false because the Rajya Sabha is never dissolved.
t: Find the statement that dissolves the permanent House.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Dissolution ends the very life of the Lok Sabha.
II. Dissolution ends the very life of the Rajya Sabha.
III. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House.
IV. Dissolution causes pending bills, motions and resolutions to lapse, subject to Article 107 rules.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: prorogation periods and adjournments of more than four consecutive days are both left out of the 60-day absence count. They are two parallel exclusions, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether two parallel rules can explain each other.

x: Option D is incorrect: prorogation ends the session but does not end pending bills; only notices lapse unless given again. Bills lapse only on dissolution.
t: Discriminate what lapses on prorogation from what lapses on dissolution.

x: Article 101(4) lets a House declare a seat vacant after 60 days' absence without permission. Article 85 covers sessions, 107 bills and 123 ordinances.
t: Recall Article 101(4) and its 60-day rule.

x: Both are true: the Constitution prescribes no minimum number of sitting days, so neither a 60-day nor a 90-day minimum exists.
t: Remember that the Constitution sets no sitting-day minimum at all.

x: In the Lok Sabha, Question Hour is the first hour, 11 AM to noon. Zero Hour follows it from noon to 1 PM.
t: Recall the order of the Lok Sabha's first two hours.

x: Both are true: Question Hour, supplementary questions and adjournment motions let Parliament question the government, follow up and raise urgent matters, which is why they make up the 'accountability triangle'. R explains A.
t: Ask whether R's functions are what make A true.

x: Starred: oral answer, with supplementaries. Unstarred: written answer, no supplementaries. Short notice: urgent matters, oral answer. Zero Hour: urgent matters without notice. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate oral from written answers, then notice from no notice.

x: Option C is incorrect: a no-confidence motion comes under Rule 198. Rule 184 is for a discussion followed by a vote. It needs 50 members' support and is allowed only in the Lok Sabha.
t: Discriminate Rule 198 (no-confidence) from Rule 184 (discussion with voting).

x: A no-confidence motion tests the ministry's majority, a confidence motion proves it, a censure motion disapproves of specific policies, and a privilege motion targets a Minister who withheld or distorted facts. The answer is a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.
t: Discriminate who moves each motion and what it aims at.

x: A is true: a censure motion must state its reasons. B is false: passing it shows political weakness but does not force the government to resign, unlike a no-confidence motion.
t: Discriminate the censure motion from the no-confidence motion.

x: J.B. Kripalani moved the first no-confidence motion, against Nehru's government in 1963.
t: Recall the first no-confidence motion's mover and year.

x: Option A is incorrect: a calling attention motion has no element of censure, unlike an adjournment motion. It draws a Minister's attention to an urgent matter, needs the presiding officer's permission and is allowed in either House.
t: Discriminate the calling attention motion from the adjournment motion.

x: Calling attention draws a Minister's notice, adjournment suspends business for an urgent matter, a privilege motion goes to the Privileges Committee, and closure (the guillotine) puts the rest to vote. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Match each device to what it does to business.

x: Once the debate time runs out, closure (the guillotine) ends the debate at once and puts all undiscussed demands or clauses to the vote together.
t: Recall what the guillotine does when time runs out.

x: A token cut reduces a demand by ₹100 to air a specific grievance. A policy cut reduces it to ₹1, and an economy cut by a specified amount.
t: Discriminate the three cut motions: ₹1, ₹100 and a specified amount.

x: Rule 184 allows a discussion on a matter of public interest that ends in a formal motion and vote. No-confidence is Rule 198 and members' urgent matters are Rule 377.
t: Discriminate Rules 184, 198 and 377.

x: Both are true: interpellation is the formal right to question the executive, and R gives its purpose, demanding explanations of government actions and policies. R explains A.
t: Ask whether R states the purpose of the right in A.

x: Both are true: in 'yielding the floor', the Speaker asks a member who is speaking to stop so another can speak, and a privilege motion is referred to the Committee of Privileges.
t: Recall each convention or motion and where it leads.

x: Three are correct: 20 starred questions a day, 30 matters under Rule 377 since 2015, and 50 members for a no-confidence motion. Statement 4 is false because Zero Hour lasts at most one hour.
t: Check each number: 20, 30, 50 and one hour.

x: A policy cut reduces a demand to ₹1 and a token cut by ₹100. A no-confidence motion needs 50 members, and Rule 377 allows 30 matters a day since 2015. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Discriminate '₹1' (policy cut) from 'by ₹100' (token cut).

x: Option D is incorrect. Since 2014, the Rajya Sabha has Zero Hour from 11 AM to noon and Question Hour from noon to 1 PM, the reverse of the Lok Sabha.
t: Remember that the Rajya Sabha's timings are the reverse of the Lok Sabha's.

x: Option D is incorrect: Zero Hour comes right after Question Hour (noon to 1 PM in the Lok Sabha), not before it. It is an informal convention lasting at most one hour.
t: Recall the order: Question Hour first, then Zero Hour.

x: If a confidence motion moved by the government is defeated, the government falls, because it has lost the Lok Sabha's support.
t: Recall the result of defeat on a confidence motion.

x: Option A is incorrect: a privilege motion does not make the government resign. It is raised against a Minister for withholding or distorting facts, needs the presiding officer's consent and goes to the Committee of Privileges.
t: Discriminate the motions that bring down a government from the others.

x: An adjournment motion carries an element of censure because it sets aside the House's business to discuss a definite, urgent matter. It is allowed only in the Lok Sabha.
t: Discriminate the adjournment motion's censure element from calling attention.

x: A no-confidence motion needs 50 members' support, a calling attention motion draws a Minister's attention without censure, an adjournment motion sets aside business for a definite urgent matter, and a privilege motion goes to the Committee of Privileges. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match each motion with its defining procedural feature.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) No-Confidence Motion
(b) Calling Attention Motion
(c) Adjournment Motion
(d) Privilege Motion

List-II
(i) Needs the support of 50 members for admission
(ii) Draws a Minister's attention to an urgent matter, with no censure
(iii) Sets aside normal business to discuss a definite urgent matter
(iv) Referred to the Committee of Privileges

Choose the correct code:

x: A member raising a matter under Rule 377 gives written notice to the Secretary-General, not to the Minister or a committee.
t: Recall where Rule 377 notices go.

x: Option B is incorrect: Rule 377 has nothing to do with no-confidence motions, which come under Rule 198 in the Lok Sabha. It lets Lok Sabha members raise urgent matters not covered by questions or motions, with written notice.
t: Discriminate Rule 377 from Rule 198.

x: A cut motion passed in the Lok Sabha shows the government has lost financial control, which amounts to a loss of confidence, so it must resign.
t: Recall why a passed cut motion counts as a loss of confidence.

x: Option A is incorrect: a policy cut reduces a demand to ₹1, showing complete disapproval of the policy. A reduction by a specified amount is an economy cut.
t: Discriminate the three cut motions: ₹1, ₹100 and a specified amount.

x: The guillotine falls when the time allotted for debate runs out, and all undiscussed demands are then voted on.
t: Recall what triggers the guillotine.

x: A is true: Lok Sabha Question Hour is 11 AM to noon. B is false: in the Rajya Sabha after 2014, noon to 1 PM is Question Hour, not Zero Hour.
t: Remember that the Rajya Sabha's timings are the reverse of the Lok Sabha's.

x: A confidence motion proves the majority, a censure motion disapproves of specific policies, a privilege motion goes to the Privileges Committee, and closure ends the debate. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match each motion to its result.

x: Both are true: a censure motion shows disapproval of specific policies, which is why its passing marks the government as politically weak even though it need not resign. R explains A.
t: Ask whether R's disapproval accounts for the weakness in A.

x: Both are true: the government moves a confidence motion, and it aims to prove the majority on the floor. The purpose does not explain who moves it, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a motion's purpose explains who moves it.

x: Both are true: Rule 184 allows a discussion that ends in a formal motion and vote, and defeat on that vote can threaten the ruling party.
t: Recall that Rule 184, unlike Rule 193, involves a vote.

x: I and II are correct: parliamentary hours and motions scrutinise government, and Question Hour is for questions to Ministers. III is false because Zero Hour is informal and needs no notice.
t: Find the statement that formalises Zero Hour.

x: Question Hour is for questions to Ministers, Zero Hour for urgent matters without notice, a confidence motion proves the majority, and Rule 184 allows a discussion with a vote. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Match each device to its purpose.

x: All four are correct: confidence motions are only for the Lok Sabha, short notice questions allow supplementaries, Zero Hour is informal, and Rule 184 involves a vote.
t: Check each statement on its own facts.

x: All four are correct: starred and unstarred questions are both taken in Question Hour and both deal with matters of general public importance. Only short notice questions are for urgent matters.
t: Discriminate general importance (starred, unstarred) from urgent importance (short notice).
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Rules relating to Starred Questions apply during Question Hour.
II. Rules relating to Unstarred Questions apply during Question Hour.
III. Starred Questions concern general public matters.
IV. Unstarred Questions concern general public matters.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Both are true: a no-confidence motion tests whether the Council of Ministers has a majority, so when it passes, the government must resign. R explains A.
t: Ask whether R's test of majority explains resigning in A.

x: Both are true: a calling attention motion has a narrower scope than an adjournment motion, and an adjournment motion needs the presiding officer's consent.
t: Compare the scope and admission of the two motions.

x: Closure (the guillotine) is used only in the Lok Sabha, mainly to put undiscussed budget demands to the vote together.
t: Recall that budget guillotine is a Lok Sabha device.

x: Question Hour and related hours exist to enforce executive accountability and control over the Council of Ministers. They are not meant to disrupt the agenda.
t: Recall the purpose of parliamentary hours.

x: Lok Sabha Question Hour is 11 AM to noon with Zero Hour after it at noon. Since 2014 the Rajya Sabha has Zero Hour at 11 AM and Question Hour from noon to 1 PM. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Remember that the Rajya Sabha reverses the Lok Sabha's order since 2014.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Question Hour in Lok Sabha
(b) Question Hour in Rajya Sabha
(c) Zero Hour in Lok Sabha
(d) Zero Hour in Rajya Sabha

List-II
(i) 12:00 Noon–1:00 PM, after Zero Hour
(ii) 12:00 Noon–1:00 PM, after Question Hour
(iii) 11:00 AM–12:00 Noon, followed by Zero Hour
(iv) 11:00 AM–12:00 Noon, followed by Question Hour

x: Option C is incorrect: Rajya Sabha Question Hour moved to noon to 1 PM after 2014, not before. Lok Sabha Question Hour stays at 11 AM to noon.
t: Recall the 2014 change in Rajya Sabha timings.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Question Hour, supplementary questions and adjournment motions make Ministers answer, follow up and face urgent debates, which is how they enforce cabinet responsibility to the legislature.
t: Ask whether R describes the mechanism that produces A.
s:
Assertion (A): Question Hour, Supplementary Questions and Adjournment Motions directly ensure cabinet responsibility to the legislature.
Reason (R): These devices let members question Ministers, follow up on their answers and set aside business for urgent matters, compelling the government to answer to the House.

x: An unstarred question gets a written answer laid on the Table, and supplementaries are not allowed. Starred questions get oral answers.
t: Discriminate written answers (unstarred) from oral answers (starred).

x: A short notice question is about a matter of urgent public importance, so it can be asked at less than the normal notice and is answered orally.
t: Recall what justifies the shorter notice.

x: Both are true: a short notice question gets an oral answer with supplementaries, and it is asked at shorter notice. The notice period does not explain the oral answer, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether the notice period explains the kind of answer.

x: Question Hour is a formal procedure under the Rules for questioning Ministers. Zero Hour is an Indian innovation for raising urgent matters without notice. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Read the label on each List-I row before matching.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Question Hour — procedural status
(b) Zero Hour — procedural status
(c) Question Hour — core purpose
(d) Zero Hour — core purpose

List-II
(i) Indian parliamentary innovation
(ii) Formal procedure under Parliamentary Rules
(iii) Questioning Ministers on administrative actions
(iv) Raising urgent matters of public importance without prior notice

x: Zero Hour began in the early 1960s as an Indian parliamentary innovation. It is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure.
t: Recall when Zero Hour began.

x: Both are true: Question Hour lasts at most one hour, and Zero Hour in the Lok Sabha usually lasts up to an hour.
t: Recall the duration of both hours.

x: The calling attention motion is an Indian innovation that does not disrupt the day's agenda. The adjournment motion is a traditional device that suspends normal business. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Read the label on each List-I row before matching.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Calling Attention Motion — origin
(b) Adjournment Motion — origin
(c) Calling Attention Motion — effect on business
(d) Adjournment Motion — effect on business

List-II
(i) Traditional parliamentary device
(ii) Indian parliamentary innovation
(iii) Does not disrupt the scheduled daily agenda
(iv) Interrupts and suspends normal parliamentary business

x: All four apply: an adjournment motion must concern a single, definite matter of recent occurrence, and only one is allowed per sitting.
t: Recall the conditions for admitting an adjournment motion.

x: A is true but R is false: Zero Hour and the calling attention motion grew out of Indian parliamentary practice; neither is mentioned in the Constitution, and Zero Hour is not even in the Rules.
t: Check whether a procedure comes from the Constitution, the Rules or convention.
s:
Assertion (A): Zero Hour and Calling Attention Motion are indigenous Indian contributions to parliamentary procedure.
Reason (R): Both are expressly provided for in the Constitution of India.

x: Question Hour, the first hour of every sitting, is for asking and answering questions to Ministers.
t: Recall what the first hour of a sitting is used for.

x: Option A is incorrect: Zero Hour is not in the Parliamentary Rules. It is an informal Indian convention, with no fixed length, held right after Question Hour.
t: Discriminate formal Question Hour from informal Zero Hour.

x: Both are true: Question Hour is set out in the Rules while Zero Hour is only a convention, and that is exactly why their status differs. R explains A.
t: Ask whether R states the difference A describes.

x: All three are correct: an adjournment motion must concern a single, definite, recent matter, cannot raise a question of privilege, and only one is allowed per sitting.
t: Recall the conditions for admitting an adjournment motion.

x: Calling attention does not disrupt the agenda and has no censure. An adjournment motion suspends business and implies censure of the government. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Contrast the two motions on disruption and censure.

x: Calling attention notices narrowed the scope of adjournment motions by offering a milder way to raise urgent matters. Question Hour and Zero Hour were not affected.
t: Recall which motion calling attention notices replaced.

x: An adjournment motion is admitted only when other routes, such as a short duration discussion, would come too late. Questions of privilege cannot be raised this way.
t: Recall the condition for admitting an adjournment motion.

x: Both are true: Zero Hour follows Question Hour in the Lok Sabha and is used to raise urgent public matters without prior notice.
t: Recall when Zero Hour falls and what it is for.

x: In the Lok Sabha, Zero Hour runs from noon to 1 PM, right after Question Hour (11 AM to noon).
t: Recall the Lok Sabha's timings.
o: The first hour of every parliamentary sitting, irrespective of the House

x: An adjournment motion aims to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance by setting aside the House's normal business. Drawing a Minister's attention is calling attention.
t: Discriminate the adjournment motion from the calling attention motion.

x: Parliamentary questions are asked in Question Hour, the first hour of every sitting.
t: Recall when questions are asked.

x: Parliamentary questions ensure executive accountability by making Ministers answer for government policies and actions.
t: Recall the purpose of parliamentary questions.

x: Parliamentary questions are mainly put to Ministers, to scrutinise administrative policy and government action.
t: Recall who answers parliamentary questions.

x: The three kinds of parliamentary question are starred, unstarred and short notice. There is no 'adjournment question'; adjournment is a motion.
t: Discriminate kinds of question from kinds of motion.

x: Option B is incorrect: at most 20 starred questions are listed for oral answer each day. A starred question has an asterisk, gets an oral answer, and allows supplementaries.
t: Recall the daily limit of 20 starred questions.

x: A starred question gets an oral answer, an unstarred question allows no supplementaries, and a short notice question is marked by its shorter notice and urgent subject. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Match each feature to its kind of question.

x: Option C is incorrect: an unstarred question has no asterisk (starred questions do). It gets a written answer laid on the Table, with no supplementaries.
t: Discriminate the asterisked starred question from the unstarred question.

x: A is true: starred and short notice questions both allow supplementaries. B is false because a short notice question gets an oral answer; only unstarred questions get written answers.
t: Discriminate oral from written answers for each kind of question.

x: I and II are correct: starred questions have an asterisk and unstarred questions do not. III is false because a short notice question is marked by its shorter notice, not an asterisk.
t: Recall how each kind of question is identified.

x: Starred questions are limited to 20 a day for oral answer and need the normal notice. Unstarred questions have no such 20-a-day limit, and short notice questions need less than normal notice. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Read the label on each List-I row before matching.
s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Starred Question — daily limit
(b) Unstarred Question — daily limit
(c) Short Notice Question — notice
(d) Starred Question — notice

List-II
(i) Standard prescribed notice
(ii) Maximum 20 questions listed per day for oral answer
(iii) Shorter than standard notice
(iv) No strict 20-per-day limit

x: Three are correct: starred questions get oral answers and an asterisk, and short notice questions concern urgent matters. Statement 2 is false because unstarred questions allow no supplementaries.
t: Check each kind of question's answer and supplementaries.

x: I, III and IV are correct: starred questions concern general importance with normal notice, and short notice questions urgent matters. II is false because unstarred questions also concern general importance.
t: Discriminate general from urgent importance.

x: Both are true: at most 20 starred questions are listed each day for oral answer, and unstarred questions have no such 20-a-day limit.
t: Recall which kind of question has the 20-a-day limit.

x: Short notice questions are listed each day at the discretion of the Speaker or Chairman, who decides whether the matter is urgent enough.
t: Recall who admits short notice questions.
